When people call climate change a hoax or a natural cycle, then say every climate model is rigged, it’s no wonder young people feel trapped between “it’s all fake” and “we’re doomed.” We need honest debate, not more panic.

Calling climate science a tax-grab conspiracy doesn’t help a teenager who’s already terrified the future is over. Scientists can be questioned without turning every projection into a hoax—or every risk into a prophecy of collapse.

I’m skeptical when politicians say climate change is just a natural cycle and scientists’ models are nonsense. But the “too late, civilization is doomed” messaging also feeds despair. We need less spin from both directions.

If the climate has always changed, why are we acting like one more policy tax will save the world? Young people are being handed doom charts and told it’s too late. Maybe question the models before surrendering to collapse talk.

Climate-policy critics call it a power grab; climate activists warn of civilizational collapse. In between, young people are left anxious and cynical. How do we talk about uncertainty without dismissing scientists or making despair the whole story?

The claim that climate change is a hoax doesn’t soothe eco-anxiety; it just turns it into a fight over who to trust. Attacking researchers won’t make the risks vanish, and doomism won’t help us respond.

When every forecast is dismissed as a scientist’s political fantasy, it’s easy to say climate change is a natural cycle and move on. But telling young people it’s all a hoax doesn’t erase their fear of the future.

My feed goes from “climate models are fake; this is a tax scheme” to “we’re past the point of no return.” No wonder people are anxious. I want less conspiracy, less apocalypse, and more room for realistic choices.

Climate policies sold with end-of-the-world language deserve scrutiny. If the science is uncertain and the models are disputed, why burden families with new taxes while young people are made to feel there’s no future anyway?

Doomism can make climate grief feel inevitable, while hoax claims and attacks on scientists make action seem pointless. Neither helps young people. We can take climate risks seriously without declaring the future already lost.

We keep hearing that climate change is a natural cycle, that scientists’ models can’t be trusted, and that policy is about control. Then we wonder why young people swing between denial and “we’re doomed.” Trust needs more than slogans.

If climate change is supposedly a hoax designed to expand government, why are so many young people grieving a future they think is gone? Maybe the answer isn’t to mock the models or tax everyone—but to stop selling both conspiracy and collapse.
